newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen focusing on data at open.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen focusing on data at open.

text.p: Wall Street is seen focusing on economic data to provide direction at Friday's opening, analysts said.

Markets will keep an eye on revised figures for the first quarter Gross Domestic Product, due out at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. A consensus estimate by economists calls for a revised rise of six percent annual growth, versus an initial 5.6 percent.
"Anything above 6.5 percent would give the market indigestion," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
Hildegard Zagorski, an analyst at Prudential Securities, said if the GDP or other figures came in out of line with predictions, "that could affect bonds and that could affect the stocks."
Other data are April new home sales, the Chicago Purchasing Managers Index and University of Michigan May consumer confidence data. All are to be released at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.
Economists forecast new home sales at 800,000 units, down from 813,000 in March. The purchasing managers' index is predicted to read 56.8 in May, down slightly from 57.2 in May.
A consensus estimate for the consumer confidence figure is 104, up from 101.4.
"I think if we should see any lower-than-expected economic strength in the data then there is a possibility the losing streak of (stocks in) the last few days could reverse," Cardillo said.
In London, the FTSE 100 was off 38 points at 4634.3. U.S. stocks were little changed.
The dollar fell in Tokyo to 116.30 yen and eased to trade against the mark at 1.6996/06 in Europe.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column reported that Morgan Stanley Group Inc and Dean Witter Discover & Co are already showing how their $10.2 billion merger will work. The merger closes this weekend.

The New York Times Market Place column reported "red chip" Chinese companies are the latest Hong Kong stock market craze. The frenzy is called tulip mania, for the passion for tulip bulbs that swept Dutch exchanges more than 350 years ago.
